answer_text:
# 🦴 Bones of the Head

The human skull is generally considered to consist of **22 bones** — **8 cranial bones** and **14 facial skeleton bones**. Some sources count up to **29 bones**, including the inner ear bones and the hyoid bone.

The skull is divided into two regions: the **neurocranium** (which protects the brain) and the **viscerocranium** (which forms the face).

---

## 🧠 Part 1: The Cranial Bones (Neurocranium) — 8 Bones

The cranium is composed of **8 bones** known as the cranial bones: the **frontal bone**, a **parietal bone** on each side, a **temporal bone** on each side, the **occipital bone**, the **ethmoid bone**, and the **sphenoid bone**.

Here is a breakdown of each:

| Bone | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Frontal Bone** | 1 | A single, seamless bone that gives your forehead its structure. |
| **Parietal Bones** | 2 | Form the sides and uppermost portion of the dome of the cranium. |
| **Temporal Bones** | 2 | Form the lower lateral sides of the skull. They subdivide into petrous, squamous, zygomatic, and mastoid parts; the petrous portion houses the inner ear. |
| **Occipital Bone** | 1 | The most posterior aspect of the skull. It has a central opening (foramen magnum) to admit the spinal cord. |
| **Sphenoid Bone** | 1 | A single bone below and in front of the brain, but behind the bones making up the face. It also forms part of the lower rear of the eye sockets. |
| **Ethmoid Bone** | 1 | Forms part of the cranial floor. |

---

## 😊 Part 2: The Facial Bones (Viscerocranium) — 14 Bones

The facial skeleton supports the soft tissues of the face. It consists of **14 bones**, which fuse to house the orbits of the eyes, the nasal and oral cavities, and the sinuses.

The bones of the facial skeleton are: the **vomer**, two **inferior nasal conchae**, two **nasal bones**, two **maxilla**, the **mandible**, two **palatine bones**, two **zygomatic bones**, and two **lacrimal bones**.

| Bone | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Mandible** | 1 | Makes up the lower jaw. It is the **only bone of the skull that moves**. |
| **Maxilla** | 2 | Form the top jaw and anchor the upper teeth. |
| **Zygomatic Bones** | 2 | The cheekbones, which join with the temporal and maxillary bones to form the zygomatic arch below the eye socket. |
| **Palatine Bones** | 2 | Form the roof of the mouth and help to form the mouth cavity. |
| **Nasal Bones** | 2 | Two small bones forming the bridge of the nose. |
| **Lacrimal Bones** | 2 | Small bones in the inner wall of the eye socket. |
| **Inferior Nasal Conchae** | 2 | Help form the nasal cavity. |
| **Vomer** | 1 | A flat bone that forms part of the nasal septum. |

---

## 🔗 How Are the Bones Connected?

Sutures are a type of fibrous joint unique to the skull. They are immovable and fuse completely around the age of 20. The main sutures are:

- **Coronal suture** – fuses the frontal bone with the two parietal bones.
- **Sagittal suture** – fuses both parietal bones to each other.
- **Lambdoid suture** – fuses the occipital bone to the two parietal bones.

The **only synovial (movable) joint** in the skull is the **temporomandibular joint (TMJ)**, a movable connection between the mandible and the temporal bone.

---

## 👶 Skull Development

In neonates, the incompletely fused suture joints give rise to membranous gaps between the bones known as **fontanelles** — the two major ones being the **frontal fontanelle** (at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures) and the **occipital fontanelle** (at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures).
